title: Beautiful Injustice
author: Afsheen Iqbal
excerpt: Equality is one of those rare words that almost no one objects to.
content: Equality is one of those rare words that almost no one objects to.It appears in constitutions, protests, classrooms, campaign speeches, and everyday conversations with remarkable ease. It has become shorthand for justice itself, as though the two were interchangeable. To advocate for equality is to occupy unquestioned moral ground; few ideals have earned such universal admiration

.The appeal is understandable. Equality feels objective. It promises consistency over prejudice, principle over preference. It suggests that fairness can be achieved through a simple rule: treat everyone the same. There is comfort in that simplicity, because simple rules ask very little of us beyond following them.Equity emerged from a different question. Rather than asking whether everyone is being treated the same, it asks whether everyone began from the same place. It recognizes that people’s lives are shaped long before any rule is applied—by circumstance, history, privilege, disability, opportunity, and countless conditions they did not choose. Where equality seeks impartiality through uniform treatment, equity seeks fairness through understanding difference. It is less concerned with identical rules than with whether those rules can ever produce just outcomes for people whose journeys were never identical to begin with.Equality promises fairness. Equity promises justice.

They sound like twins. They often stand on the same podium, march under the same slogans, and occupy the same speeches. Yet, when asked to solve the same problem, they frequently choose different answers.Their disagreement begins with a deceptively simple question: What does it actually mean to be fair?If fairness means treating everyone identically, equality appears sufficient. But if fairness means ensuring that people can genuinely reach the same opportunities despite profoundly different starting points, equality alone begins to show its limits.Imagine two children standing before a table. A loaf of bread is placed between them, and the adult responsible for serving it cuts it into two perfectly equal halves. One child receives one piece; the other receives the second. There are no larger slices, no special treatment, no accusations of favoritism. The division is exact. It is difficult to imagine a fairer way to distribute something that both children want.

There is something deeply reassuring about moments like these. Equality transforms fairness into arithmetic. It replaces judgment with measurement, allowing justice to appear objective rather than personal. No one has to decide who deserves more or less because the decision has already been made: everyone receives the same.But fairness begins to look different once the story continues. One child has not eaten since yesterday. The other finished lunch less than an hour ago. The bread has been divided equally, yet the need it was meant to satisfy was never equal in the first place.Similarly, if two students earn the same grade, but one studied in an air-conditioned private school with unlimited tutors while the other studied by candlelight after working to help support their family, should both be judged as though they travelled the same road?Again, imagine a company where, for decades, almost every leadership position has been occupied by men. To address this imbalance, the company introduces a policy: for every ten management positions it fills, at least four must go to qualified women. Immediately, some employees object. “If men and women are equal,” they argue, “why should women have reserved places? Shouldn’t every position simply go to the best candidate, regardless of gender?” At first glance, the criticism seems reasonable. Equality demands the same rules for everyone.But the policy was never created because women were less capable. It was created because, for years, equally capable women had fewer opportunities to reach those positions in the first place. The quota does not assume women deserve success more than men; it acknowledges that the competition itself has not always been equal.And yet, despite these realities, equity rarely enjoys the same instinctive acceptance as equality.
People seldom ask whether equality is fair.They ask whether equity is.

There is something unsettling about a principle that refuses to give everyone the same answer. We are taught from childhood that fairness means sameness—that every child gets the same slice, every student follows the same rules, every competitor begins at the same whistle. Equity disrupts that instinct. It suggests that fairness sometimes requires different decisions for different people, and that proposition is far less emotionally comfortable than equal treatment ever was.

It is this discomfort that gives rise to some of the most difficult questions. If fairness sometimes requires treating people differently, how different is too different? If some people receive support that others do not, when does justice become favoritism? If the past has shaped today’s inequalities, how much of the past should today’s decisions attempt to correct? Can fairness ever be achieved if identical treatment is no longer the rule? And if every person’s circumstances are unique, is there any point at which we stop making exceptions?

These are not easy questions, nor are they questions that equity can afford to ignore. They are the very questions that determine whether equity is a deeper form of justice—or merely another way of creating inequality.Perhaps, then, the question was never whether equality is good or bad. Equality remains one of humanity’s greatest moral achievements. A world without it would be one where prejudice openly replaced principle, where laws bent according to wealth, power, or identity. The answer is not to abandon equality, but to recognize its limits.
Equality asks us to begin at the same rule.Equity asks us to begin with the same humanity.

One protects us from arbitrary discrimination; the other reminds us that identical treatment alone cannot erase unequal lives. Justice demands both. Equality gives justice its consistency. Equity gives it its conscience.

Perhaps our greatest mistake has never been believing in equality. It has been believing that equality, by itself, is always enough. For there is a profound difference between giving everyone the same chance and giving everyone a genuine chance to succeed. The first satisfies our desire for symmetry; the second asks us to confront reality.
Fairness has never been as simple as dividing a loaf of bread into equal halves. It has always demanded the courage to ask a harder question: What does this person need for this to truly be fair?
Justice, after all, was never meant to be beautiful.
It was meant to be just.
editorsNote: A patient argument that distinguishes equal treatment from the harder work of equitable justice.

title: The Saint on the Hill
author: Zohara H. Khan
excerpt: We know of the soul that breathed new life into Sylhet.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Saint on the Hill
content: We know of the soul that breathed new life into Sylhet. Of the caravan that brought him to the subcontinent of India all the way from Konya. Of the man that tasted the soil of Sylhet and found it reminiscent of the sacred earth of Makkah, choosing to make this land his home.

We know of Hazrat Shah Jalal, the saint that brought a new of era into the land of Sylhet, whose name is etched into the history of this scared region, where the streets sing songs of him seven centuries later still.

But history is like a lantern. It follows the figure on the front, shining brightly atop his head as generations come to commemorate him, but not those that followed behind him. Today, we have schools, universities, airports and cities dedicated in his name, but fewer remember the ones that helped make Sylhet what it is today.

Yet, the hills of Khadim Nagar tell a different story. Of a man that walked where the lantern did not shine. Of a man that arrived not with riches or gold and an army at his beck and call, but with a heart full of devotion to God and a mission to preach Islam.
That hill, sings the name of Hazrat Shah Farhan, or as Bangladeshi’s like to call him, Hazrat Shah Poran (RA).

I made my home in Khadim Nagar. In this hill that still remembers the saint that helped make Sylhet what it is today. But like many, I too had little knowledge of who this said saint was. Like many, I marveled at the stories of Shah Jalal and his conquest, but never bothered to shed light on those following behind him.
Until I saw the hill for myself.
The questions did come all at once, but gradually as my curiosity grew. But the first of them all was, who is the man buried on that hill?
Before it became a place of prayer and devotion, that hill had been but a silent home for a traveler that had left his birth land miles away to make this place his new home.

According to scholars, Hazrat Shah Paran was the nephew of Hazrat Shah Jalal, son to his sister about whom little is known. Born in 1271, far from the lush greenery of Sylhet in the lands of Hadhramaut, Yemen, though some historians believe the land of origins was like that of his Uncle, Konya, present day Turkey.

At the mere age of 11, Shah Paran lost his father in the year of 1281, becoming the ward of his grandfather, Syed Ahmed Kabir Shurawardi, who spent the rest of his life teaching Shah Paran to become the man he would be remembered for. Once he was in the ripe age to be a young man, Shah Paran decided to join his uncle in the expedition to the Indian Subcontinent.

Little is known about the exact time of departure, but what is known for sure, is that in the year of 1303, the band of preachers finally made their way into the heart of the region that would shape all of their futures- Sylhet.

From this moment on, I already knew the story. I knew about Burhanuddin, the man who had his baby murdered before his eyes merely because the akika ceremony for his son upset Raja Gaur Govinda. About the tears of justice, he shed to Sultan Shamsuddin Firuz Shah of Bengal.

The conquest of Sylhet thus began, but it did not end in the first attempt. The first to lead the campaign was Sikander Khan Ghazi, but he failed miserably. So, the sultan sent Nasiruddin with an army, and it was during his campaign did he come across the band of dervishes from Konya, led by Shah Jalal, which was the turning point for the army who now held a spiritual allegiance for the conquest of the sacred lands of Sylhet.
I knew this much alright, but the real question was, what was the role of the man buried on that hill? And how is he significant to it?

Shah Paran took part in the conquest alongside his uncle. There is no record of him that describes him fighting the Raja gallantly, or a commander that saved Sylhet with an army of three thousand. It would be fun to read such a record, could also explain all the admiration people had when visiting the hill, but that was not the case.
Shah Paran, like his uncle, helped restore a lost glory back to Sylhet, pronouncing it one of the scared lands of Islam. Like the rest of Shah Jalal’s followers, Shah Paran merely did his job.
So why is he revered so?

After the conquest, the band dervishes began to disperse, their mission in Sylhet having been fulfilled. While some went home, some scattered across the continent, and fewer still chose to stay, to make Sylhet their new home. One among them was Shah Paran.

History did not revere him because he was a gallant warrior that fought like Zulfiqar had come to life, but because he was one that chose to stay. The one that believed in the people of Sylhet, in the vision his Uncle had, and decided to protect and guide the people residing there.

And like him, those who remained began settling in different corners of the region, establishing khanqahs, teaching the Qur'an, guiding communities, and planting the seeds of a spiritual tradition that would flourish for centuries. The story of Sylhet was never written by one saint alone. It was carried forward by an entire brotherhood of dervishes, each leaving behind a legacy of his own, names like Shah Ma'lum and Tajuddin Quraishi, men I would come to know only as my curiosity deepened.

Among those names however, one lingered the most, perhaps because hisw final resting place was right where I called my own home. Perhaps because the path that led him there was not because of his triumph in the conquest, but because of what followed after wards.
Of the debated story regarding the jalali pigeons, and how that one mistake would go on to shape the rest of his future, and that of Khadim Nagar.
History is indeed like a lantern.

It shines upon one figure the brightest while the ones following behind him are left in the shadows. But perhaps they are not in the shadows after all. They are not in the limelight either, but perhaps somewhere where they await someone to share their story.

Hazrat Shah Farhan, or commonly known as Hazrat Shah Paran (RA) would go on to spend the rest of his life at his khanqah atop the hill in Khadim Nagar, never marrying. The young traveler that crossed continents for his uncle in pursuit of faith. The dervish that chose humility over disappointment. He’d spend the rest of his life devoting his time in spreading the message of Islam to the people of Sylhet, offering shelter to those in need, leaving a legacy that his thrived and inspired for centuries.

So, the next time I find myself walking through Khadim Nagar, through the shrine atop the hill, I’ll know it isn’t just a story of a dervish who helped shape Sylhet from a place where the lantern light had already faded.
It’s the story of a saint that chose to stay.
editorsNote: An essay that shifts historical attention from the celebrated figure to the people and places beyond the lantern light.

title: Cannibal
author: Mahia Zaman Mounata
excerpt: War feeds on nations; hunger feeds on men—until the starving can no longer tell whether they are victims, survivors, or cannibals.
content: Dedicated to Palestine
War feeds on nations; hunger feeds on men—until the starving can no longer tell whether they are victims, survivors, or cannibals.

I do not remember the day we stopped being counted as men and became, instead, numbers on a list that grew shorter by the week. I remember only that one morning I woke and found I could see my own ribs through my shirt, as though the shirt itself had grown transparent from hunger, and I thought: this is not so bad, I can still see. There are men who cannot see anymore. I considered this a kind of fortune.

They kept us in the low building behind the works, where the machines had once made something — I never learned what, and by the time I arrived the machines were silent, gutted, their bellies opened and picked clean of anything that might be sold or melted or eaten, though of course metal cannot be eaten, we had tried. I had tried. I had put a screw in my mouth once, only to feel its shape, only to remember that my mouth still had a function beyond breathing.

Each morning they lined us in the yard and each morning the line was shorter, and no one asked where the missing had gone, because to ask was to invite the question to turn and look at you, and none of us wanted to be looked at. I stood between a man named Pavel, who had once been fat and now wore his old fatness like a coat two sizes too large, folds of skin hanging where flesh had been, and a boy whose name I never learned because he stopped speaking in the second week and never started again.

They did not need whips. Hunger is a whip that never tires, that needs no arm to swing it. But they used whips anyway, I think because a whip is a sound, and sound reminds a man that he is still a subject and not yet a corpse, and perhaps this too was a mercy, though I did not think of it as mercy then. I thought of nothing then except the next mouthful, and after the next mouthful, the one after that, and in this way a man's whole mind can be reduced to an arithmetic of small forward motions, one gram, one gram, one gram.
Then came the day they stopped bringing the ration at all.

We waited by the door the way animals wait, without dignity, because dignity is the first thing hunger sells and the price is always fair, always exactly what you can afford, which is to say everything. Pavel did not wait long. On the third day of nothing he simply lay down in the corner and did not rise, and on the fourth day two men I did not know went to him with a tenderness that sickened me more than any violence I had witnessed, because it was the tenderness of men handling something precious, something they had waited a long time for.
I told myself I would not watch. I watched.

I told myself I would not partake. I do not remember deciding otherwise. I remember only the taste, which was not the taste of triumph or even of relief, but simply the taste of continuing, the way water tastes of nothing except that it lets you go on being thirsty tomorrow instead of never again.

And when it came to be my turn — when the fever took me in the sixth week and I did not rise, and I felt hands lift my arm the way I had once lifted Pavel's, weighing it, considering it — I understood that I had become, without ever choosing it, both the feast and the guest at the feast, the eaten and the eater, and that there was no arithmetic left that could tell me which one I truly was.
And I watched them eat the flesh of them, I ate mine too. My.. own... Flesh. Did I also become a cannibal?
editorsNote: A stark first-person account of hunger and survival that refuses an easy division between victim and transgressor.

title: Don’t Call Us Pretty, Call Us Medusa
author: Afia Ayman
excerpt: I was terrified when I first learned of Medusa.
imageAlt: Cover image for Don’t Call Us Pretty, Call Us Medusa
content: I was terrified when I first learned of Medusa. The myth of the snake-headed monster scared me enough to avoid her real story. I was taught to fear the hiss, and the cold eyes that turned men to stone. It is easy enough to feed off the fear, but deep down, I knew I wanted to excavate the truth. The stone-cold floor of the temple. Her sanctity violated by the god of the sea, because gods never learned how to take “no” for an answer. The silence of a deity was louder than her scream for help. Whose name do you cry, when the very goddess you worshiped turns her back and fails to protect? The silk hair that turned into thousands of snakes were not her enemies, but sentinels. A crown of hissing truth that petrified the men who came to hunt her down. They say villains aren’t born, they are carved by the hands of those around you. Men were vengeful enough to behead a victim just to obliterate their own kind.

The muted mercy of a goddess gave birth to patriarchy. They needed a monster, so the gods could keep their names clean. Labelling medusa as a monster was easier to validate the action of those who wanted to benefit off of the entity. And I would like to clarify that the entity is, unequivocally, men. Cause it is very humane to want to justify their own acts, regardless of how vile their actions can be. The root of demonizing women is dated back much earlier than we think. It is painfully ironic that female figures are often mistaken as a fragile and vulnerable being where expressing emotions like anger, hunger and ambition are considered as monstrosity.

Medusa’s traditional story is a classic case of victim blaming, where a survivor of assault is punished for the vile act that was committed against her. Her story raises few concerns and questions in my chaotic mind. Our body is a vessel of our soul. Even though they exist in separate forms, body and souls are intertwined and linked like twins growing inside a mother’s womb. Therefore, when a body is violated, the disgusts, the resistance, the anger, the protest, the pain run deep into our blood and reach to our soul, cuts through it and linger there. The myth of Medusa is a mirror to this human nature.

Isn’t it horrible enough that a fellow human being is capable of causing so much destruction and annihilation to another human being, that living through each day can feel like a thousand deaths you have to conquer just to survive. And when your soul is a wreck cause of all the damages that have been done to it, your own body becomes an unfamiliar refuge.

But when we dig a little deeper, a radical rebellion emerges shifting our perspective, illustrating that Athena might not be the villain of this myth, but a savior. What if Athena chose to display her mercy and favors in a way the patriarchal eye could not immediately comprehend? What if Athena turned medusa into a monster so that no men or male god could survive her powerful gaze or never be able to harm her again!

This tactical intervention directly dismantles what film theorist Laura Mulvey famously coined the “male gaze”. The term “male gaze” depicts men as active observers (those who hold power and control the narratives) and women as passive objects (who are meant to be consumed and to be looked at as desirable objects). Athena flipped the script by giving medusa the gaze that turned men into stone which is an act of self-defense against patriarchy. In a world where women are expected to be silent and docile, medusa symbolizes power so strong that makes you pause before you think of messing with the figure. Goddess Athena turned medusa into a completely different entity where the snakes in her head were not enemies but her savior, her sentinels. That is what I call protection. Like a shelter that tends to protect you from feasible harm, Athena saved her like a patron. Just as a mother who would do anything to protect her child, Athena turned the curse into a “gift of armor”.

Men who like to address themselves as so called protectors, patriarchy is a system designed to validate their own conquests. A society that loves to feed off of the fear and insecurities of women, being able to express raw emotions like anger, frustration and rejecting the superficial beauty standards is an act of rebellion. The monstrosity itself is the real illusion of the narrative. Medusa, is not lethal as the story portrayed her to be. Instead, as the philosopher Hélène Cixous so beautifully noted, Medusa is laughing and beautiful. Her laughter is a declaration of survival and an echo of relief. For the sake of a violent society, we must cease expecting survivors to stay frail. Do not demand our gentleness when the world is still full of predators. Do not ask us to be compliant, and don't call us pretty. Call us Medusa.
editorsNote: A forceful re-reading of Medusa that asks who benefits when a survivor is named a monster.

title: Mnemosyne of Oneiroi
author: Mahia Zaman
excerpt: Phren has, for some time, been occupied by a recurring phenomenon.
imageAlt: Cover image for Mnemosyne of Oneiroi
content: Phren has, for some time, been occupied by a recurring phenomenon.
The phenomenon concerns a face.

It would be inaccurate to claim that the face appears frequently. In truth, its appearances are irregular and separated by intervals long enough to cast doubt upon its existence. Yet each reappearance possesses a peculiar authority, as though the intervening years had been merely a brief interruption.
The difficulty lies in description

No feature can be recalled with certainty. Attempts at reconstruction invariably fail. The eyes cannot be remembered. The mouth cannot be remembered. Even the distinction between youth and age becomes impossible to determine.
Nevertheless, recognition occurs immediately.
This presents a contradiction. Ordinarily, one recognizes a face because one remembers it. In this case, recognition precedes memory.
The face is familiar before it is known.
It may belong to a forgotten individual encountered long ago. It may represent several people condensed into one. It may be entirely fictitious.
None of these explanations are satisfactory.
For they fail to account for the peculiar feeling accompanying the appearance of the face: namely, the impression that it remembers Phren more clearly than Phren remembers it.
This impression persists after waking.
Indeed, it is often stronger during waking hours than within the dream itself.
The dream fades. The familiarity remains.
A further observation must be noted.

Most dreams vanish because they lack sufficient weight to survive consciousness. This face appears to obey the opposite principle. The dream surrounding it is forgotten first, as though memory sacrifices all other details to preserve this single fragment.
The result is unfortunate.
Phren now possesses a memory detached from its origin.
A recognition without identification.
A certainty without evidence.
The condition would be easier to endure if the face inspired fear. Fear possesses a recognizable object. One may flee from it, confront it, or explain it.
The face inspires none.
What it inspires is responsibility.
Responsibility for what remains unknown.
It is possible that this entire matter is insignificant. Dreams are notoriously deceptive, and memory is often guilty of manufacturing importance where none exists.
Yet this explanation encounters a final difficulty.
The face has never asked to be remembered.
The face has never asked to be remembered.
And still, after all these years, it remains.
One is therefore compelled to consider an alternative possibility:
that memory is not preserving the face.
The face is preserving the memory
editorsNote: A quiet philosophical fiction that makes the instability of memory its central mystery.

title: A Daughter’s Deadline
author: Zohara H. Khan
excerpt: What is chosen freely carries meaning. What is imposed carries weight.
imageAlt: Cover image for A Daughter’s Deadline
content: What is chosen freely carries meaning. What is imposed carries weight.

It’s something that has been nagging at my brain for quite some time. The idea of marriage. When chosen on your own, it’s something that holds the utmost meaning in your life. But when it is imposed, it becomes a burden to carry. Yes, the matter has settled quite comfortably in my mind. Perhaps because I have turned twenty-two, and according to the people around me, I’m very much ready to be married off.
But the question is, what makes one ‘ready’ to be married off?
What is chosen freely carries meaning. What is imposed carries weight.

As the last child of six children, I had watched all my siblings get married off, and in every single one of them, there was a lesson I learnt. They all married men from different families, different backgrounds, different jobs, and certainly different personalities. But they all had one thing in common. Not the men they married, but ‘how’ they married.

They were all told that the time to be wed had come before they were even ready. Where they considered too old? No. They were but in the early twenties. Were there nasty rumors circulating about them? No. They were clean as a slate. Were the awfully poor? Not really. They had food on the table three times.
So why?

Was it because women often tend to have less chances at marriage when they are older? Or that she was to be wed off to a respectable man before her name was somehow tainted? Maybe, those were all the reasons.
But what if she is still studying and wants to study higher?
Oh, no need for that. The education she had is enough. Women need only study to be worthy of their husband, not worthy for a career.
What if she doesn’t like the husband we chose?
That is alright. Love blooms after marriage anyway. She will eventually fall for him.
What if he doesn’t like her?
Not necessary. So long as she fulfills her duties as a wife and gives him children, he will be satisfied with her. Love is not important.
How often have we heard these sentences?
A girl is old enough to marry, but too young to decide who to marry. How old is too old, and how young is too young?
How often, was a girl rushed to the folds of marriage before she even knew what was going on? And mainly, why?
For the society? Family pressure? That having a daughter unmarried for too long can be considered scandalous? That she’s unwanted? Undesired?
What is chosen freely carries meaning. What is imposed carries weight.

Society often brings that up, when the said girl’s own family has these worries. When public opinion is all they can think of, and the happiness and stability of their daughter’s future falls in the hands of outsiders. When public validation starts meaning more than the dreams and hopes a girl has to bury under the ground.
And when a girl does end up marrying late, well… that’s a whole different story.
Desire becomes secondary.
Refusal becomes rebellion.
Delay becomes deviance.
The scandalous daughter. The abomination of a child.
Be it today, yesterday, in the 21st century, or a thousand years ago. The story of south Asian women does not change.
“What is chosen freely carries meaning. What is imposed carries weight.”
Always the daughter, never the son.
The pressure of being the woman of a South Asian household.
Marriage is considered a choice. But if it becomes socially mandatory, is it still considered a choice?
editorsNote: A personal essay that examines how family and social pressure can turn marriage from a choice into a deadline.

title: The Witness
author: Mahia Zaman Mounata
excerpt: The first thing I noticed about her was that she seemed strangely untouched by the room.
content: The first thing I noticed about her was that she seemed strangely untouched by the room.

The chair beneath her was old. The walls were stained with age. Dust floated through the afternoon light like tiny lost souls. Yet none of it appeared to belong to her. She sat there as though she had arrived from somewhere else entirely.
I was supposed to be listening
Instead, I found myself staring.
She was beautiful in a way that made me uncomfortable—not because beauty itself is frightening, but because it seemed impossible that such beauty could exist beside such sadness.
For a moment I forgot where I was.
I forgot that she was sitting in front of me.
I almost felt as though I had wandered into her world rather than invited her into mine.
Then she began speaking.
“I still remember the day I got my first period,” she said.
The sentence sounded ordinary.
Almost childish.
“I thought my life was over.”
A faint smile crossed her face.
“My mother explained that it would happen every month. Every month. As if that were a reasonable thing to tell someone.”
She laughed softly.
“There was the pain, of course. The stomach cramps. The headaches. The exhaustion. The dizziness. The strange feeling that my body had declared war on itself.”
She lowered her eyes.
“But that wasn’t the worst part.”
“The worst part was realizing what came with being a woman.”
The room seemed colder.
“I belonged to a conservative Muslim family. I dressed modestly. I covered my hair. I covered my body. I followed every rule that was given to me.”
She paused.
“It never mattered.”
I frowned.
“What do you mean?”
She looked at me.
“The eyes.”
Her answer was immediate.
“The eyes always found me.”
She folded her hands together.
“No matter how much I covered myself, I could feel them. On buses. On streets. In markets. In classrooms.”
Her voice became quieter.
“Sometimes I wondered if becoming invisible was the only way to be safe.”
Outside, a bird struck the window and flew away.
Neither of us reacted.
“One afternoon I was returning home from tuition.”
The words came slowly.
“The bus was crowded at first.”
I listened carefully.
“Then people began leaving.”
One stop.
Then another.
Then another.
Until she was alone.
“The sun was still shining,” she said.
“I remember that part clearly.”
Her fingers tightened around each other.
“People always imagine darkness.”
She shook her head.
“But terrible things happen in daylight too.”
The silence stretched.
“The bus took a wrong turn.”
Something inside me tightened.
“I knew it was wrong immediately.”
She looked toward the window.
“I remember thinking that maybe I was mistaken.”
A weak smile.
“Human beings are talented at lying to themselves.”
The room felt smaller now.
The air heavier.
“I tried to leave.”
She swallowed.
“I tried to scream.”
Her voice faltered.
“I tried to fight.”
Then she looked directly at me.
“People always ask whether I resisted.”
The smile vanished.
“No one asks why resistance wasn’t enough.”
I could not answer.
She continued.
“The days that followed stopped making sense.”
A shadow passed across her face.
“There was a room.”
She paused.
“A room where time became sick.”
I didn’t understand.
Neither, apparently, did she.
“Morning and night stopped existing. Hours stopped existing. Sometimes I woke up. Sometimes I lost consciousness.”
Her gaze drifted somewhere far beyond the walls.
“They came and went.”
The sentence was simple.
That made it worse.
“They treated suffering like entertainment.”
Her voice remained calm.
Too calm.
“As though another human being could be reduced to an object.”
She rubbed her hands together absentmindedly.
“I was beaten when I spoke.”
A pause.
“Beaten when I remained silent.”
Another pause.
“Mocked when I cried.”
The room seemed impossibly quiet.
“They laughed.”
For some reason that single detail felt heavier than everything else.
“They laughed while I begged.”
Her eyes grew distant.
“I remember realizing something.”
“What?”
“That cruelty does not always come from anger.”
I stared at her.
She continued.
“Sometimes people hurt others because they enjoy having power.”
The words settled into the room like stones.
“They wanted fear.”
She looked at me.
“So eventually I stopped giving it to them.”
I blinked.
“What do you mean?”
A tired smile appeared.
“I left.”
I frowned.
“You escaped?”
She shook her head.
“No.”
The smile remained.
“I left before my body did.”
For the first time, I didn’t know what she meant.
But somehow I understood.
“The mind can only carry so much pain,” she whispered.
“So one day it begins walking away.”
The room seemed darker now.
The sunlight had vanished.
Or perhaps I had stopped seeing it.
“I stopped counting the days.”
She stared at the floor.
“I stopped hoping.”
A pause.
“I stopped being afraid.”
Another pause.
“And then I stopped being alive.”
The sentence arrived gently.
Almost peacefully.
No tears.
No anger.
No dramatic conclusion.
Simply a fact.
The way someone might describe rain.
Or winter.
Or the setting of the sun.
Then she stopped speaking.
And suddenly something felt wrong.
Very wrong.
I looked around.
The room no longer resembled my office.
The walls were gone.
The furniture was gone.
The air smelled metallic.
Heavy.
Unnatural.
A strange ringing filled my ears.
I blinked.
Once.
Twice.
And then I understood.
Till she was finished with her story, I realized I was standing right in front of her.
Her dead body.
A beauty turned into something the human mind refused to recognize.
Was I crying? Was I shocked? Was I traumatized? Was I dreaming? I don’t know. I don’t know who she is. I just know she was just like me.
But the good news is she was lifeless. Finally dead.
She was in peace. The suffering has ended.
I sat there staring blankly.
Was she me?
editorsNote: A measured narrative about testimony, trauma, and what it means to listen closely to another person.

title: The Monster Was Always the Monster: What Frankenstein Gets Right About Ugliness and Evil
author: onu
excerpt: Mary Shelley’s novel raises a question we’ve been too polite to answer honestly.
imageAlt: Illustration accompanying an essay on Frankenstein
content: We’ve been told our whole lives that beauty is only skin deep. What matters is who you are on the inside. That judging someone by their appearance is shallow, primitive, and morally wrong.
Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein quietly, methodically, and devastatingly dismantles this comfortable lie.

When Victor Frankenstein assembles his creature from the parts of corpses and animates it in a burst of scientific hubris, he intends to create something beautiful. He selects the finest components. He labored for two years.

What emerges is an eight-foot monstrosity — yellow skin stretched thin over visible musculature, watery eyes, features assembled from the dead. So hideous that Victor abandons it immediately upon seeing it breathe.
Here’s the thing that made me stop reading.
The creature, at least in the beginning, is good.

It rescues a drowning girl — and gets shot for its trouble by her guardian who sees only the horror of its face. It secretly performs chores for a family living in the woods — chopping firewood, shoveling snow — falling in love with their warmth from a distance. It waits patiently for the right moment to introduce itself. That moment comes when the family’s blind father is left alone. Unable to see the creature, the father converses with it normally. A friendship begins to form.
Then the children return. They see the creature. They drive it away violently.
It is only after these repeated rejections — after being denied recognition, companionship, and basic humanity — that the creature turns to murder, vengeance, and destruction.

And even then, the creature tells us it feels remorse. Unlike Satan from Paradise Lost, who declares evil be thou my good, or Iago from Othello, who revels in wickedness without a trace of guilt, the creature still carries an ethical compass, however broken. It knows what it does is wrong. It just cannot stop itself.
So, how does ugliness turn an otherwise good soul wicked?
The most intuitive answer is social.

Victor abandoned the creature like an absent father. Society rejected it purely on the basis of appearance. That rejection bred resentment. Resentment curdled into evil. Under this reading, the creature is a victim of lookism — society’s irrational prejudice against the ugly — and if only people had treated it as the blind father was beginning to, it might have lived an entirely different life.

This reading is compelling. It maps almost perfectly onto the modern psychology of incels — men who, unable to receive romantic recognition largely because of their appearance, develop a deep social resentment that occasionally erupts into real-world violence. What the incel wants, and what the creature wants, isn’t purely physical. It’s recognition. It’s to be seen as belonging.

The creature even makes this explicit. When it corners Victor and demands he build a female companion, it specifies: make her as ugly as me. Not beautiful. Ugly. Because only with someone equally excommunicated from society could the creature feel secure that it would not be abandoned again.

Mary Shelley, writing in the Romantic tradition, and daughter of feminist pioneer Mary Wollstonecraft, was naturally drawn to this explanation. Both movements traced the origin of human suffering not to immutable human nature but to the changeable habits, biases, and prejudices of society. The monster is evil because society made it so.
But this reading runs into two serious problems.

The first: even if society’s prejudice against ugliness caused the creature’s evil, what if that prejudice is itself innate and immutable? The creature actually tests this. Reasoning that adults have been corrupted by society’s biases, it decides to befriend a child — someone not yet poisoned by prejudice. It approaches a boy alone.
The boy’s response: Let me go, monster, ugly wretch. You wish to eat me and tear me to pieces. You are an ogre.
No one taught this child to fear ugliness. No cultural conditioning is required. The revulsion appears to be built in.
The second problem is deeper. What if the connection between ugliness and wickedness isn’t external at all?

Enter physiognomy — a discipline so thoroughly discredited today that most people have never heard of it, yet so seriously regarded throughout Western history that Plato held physiognomic views, a treatise on the subject is attributed to Aristotle’s school, and it was considered a legitimate science well into the nineteenth century.
Physiognomy holds that the outer form — particularly the face — reveals the inner character. It does not determine it. Reveals it.

Its eighteenth-century peak came with Johann Lavater, whose Essays on Physiognomy was an international bestseller. Mary Shelley’s father almost certainly read it. Shelley herself almost certainly did too. Its influence on Frankenstein is unmistakable.
The physiognomic reading of Frankenstein is this: ugliness does not cause wickedness through the external mechanism of social rejection. It indicates that the soul was already wicked.

Under this reading, we should be suspicious of how the creature narrates its own story. Victor repeatedly warns us — the creature is eloquent and deceitful. Its claims to have been pure and gentle in the beginning, its expressions of remorse at the end — these may be exactly what a sophisticated, self-aware monster would say.
Shelley gives us two characters who support this reading strongly.

Elizabeth, Victor’s adopted sister, is described in deeply physiognomic terms — golden hair, clear brow, blue eyes expressive of sensibility and sweetness. Lavater believed the eyes and brows most revealed inner character. Elizabeth’s noble appearance maps perfectly onto a noble, gentle, virtuous woman throughout the novel. She eventually turns out to be not a peasant’s child at all, but the abandoned daughter of a Milanese nobleman — the classic literary trope of noble appearance signaling noble blood.

Justine, the maidservant, is also beautiful — and also ethical, gentle, and kind even when wrongfully accused and sentenced to death for crimes she did not commit. Here is the crucial counterpoint: Justine receives no recognition. She is exiled by society. She suffers unjustly. And yet she shows no indication whatsoever of turning toward evil.
The social reading cannot explain Justine.

What about Victor himself — handsome, yet cowardly and selfish? Lavater never claimed moral determinism. He claimed revelation. Essence can be overcome — rarely, but it can. The greatest example in Western philosophy: Socrates, famously ugly, with a soul of extraordinary beauty. Nietzsche recounts the story of a face-reader who visited Athens and told Socrates to his face that he was a monster harboring terrible vices. Socrates answered simply: you know me, sir. He agreed. When young, he had been vicious, lustful, gluttonous. His philosophical practice overcame what his face revealed. His essence, not his destiny.
Frankenstein is usually read as a cautionary tale about scientific hubris, about playing God, about the dangers of abandoning what we create.
But its deeper provocation is this: maybe we are not obsessed enough with appearances. Or at least, we don’t take appearances seriously enough.

By treating the surface as completely disconnected from the soul, we have lost an entire vocabulary for reading the world. The Greeks, the Christians, the early moderns — virtually every tradition in Western intellectual history treated the beauty of something as a genuine indicator of its proper functioning and goodness. We are the historical outliers who insist on the complete separation of form and essence.

I am not arguing that physiognomy is correct. I am arguing that it is significant — that the intuition it points toward, the felt connection between outward form and inward character, has survived across millennia of human experience for some reason. That when the creature is assembled from death and emerges monstrous, Shelley is not just describing a social problem waiting to be solved by more enlightened attitudes.
She may be describing something older and harder than that.
The monster was always the monster.
Its ugliness did not make it so.
It was always already there — waiting, like a latent seed, for the conditions that would let it bloom.
If you want to explore the other side of this argument — how beauty can elevate rather than merely reveal — Plato’s Symposium is the place to go.
editorsNote: A provocative reading of Shelley’s creature that tests the boundary between social rejection and moral nature.
